question: How explicitly is the run's premise stated in the first 30 seconds?
pole_low: Drops straight into play and lets the goal emerge
pole_high: States the full challenge, rules, and win condition up front
why: Premise-first framing makes a run instantly legible to a young viewer; emergent framing rewards patience. It decides how the avatar opens every session.
evidence_needed: Transcripts of the first 30s of 3 videos per creator: is a goal/rules statement present, and how complete is it?

question: Does the creator engineer the spectacle or discover it?
pole_low: Plays straight and reacts to whatever the game produces
pole_high: Deliberately builds the setup so a collapse, crash, or explosion is guaranteed
why: This is the Disaster Engineer axis: an avatar that stages experiments behaves and talks completely differently from one that witnesses accidents.
evidence_needed: Segments where a big physics event occurs: was it set up on camera beforehand, or accidental? Tally per creator.

question: Is excitement a constant high level or a peaks-and-valleys wave?
pole_low: Energy rises and falls with the action, with genuinely quiet stretches
pole_high: Near-constant high energy and volume regardless of what is happening
why: Constant hype reads as zero dead air to young viewers but exhausts over a long coached session; wave energy makes peaks mean something. This sets the avatar's baseline dial.
evidence_needed: Word-rate and volume proxies across full videos, sampled in quiet gameplay stretches vs action stretches.

question: When something breaks or a run collapses, is the failure the payoff or a setback?
pole_low: Failure is a problem: recover, retry, get back on plan
pole_high: Failure is the product: the collapse is celebrated as the best moment of the video
why: In physics-sandbox shows the wreck often IS the win. An avatar on the high end never apologises for a disaster; on the low end it treats it as a mistake to fix.
evidence_needed: Failure segments: creator's immediate reaction framing (celebration vs frustration vs retry talk) in the 10s after a collapse or death.

question: Does the creator commentate from outside the game or play a character inside it?
pole_low: Pure commentator: talks about the game, the plan, and the audience
pole_high: In character: speaks as a role (officer, captain, citizen) and improvises scenes with others
why: OMB-style roleplay is a wholly different avatar skill — scene partner, not narrator. Where the avatar sits decides what its lines even are.
evidence_needed: Sample dialogue turns in Roblox/roleplay videos: proportion of in-character speech vs meta commentary.

question: What is the humour aimed at: the system and NPCs, or the creator themselves?
pole_low: Self-directed: the joke is the creator's mistake, panic, or bad idea
pole_high: Outward: the joke is what the game, its physics, or its characters suffer
why: Gray-style gleeful chaos and family-friendly self-deprecation produce opposite personalities. For a middle-school product this axis must be measured, then deliberately capped.
evidence_needed: Code the target of each laugh beat in sampled segments: self, game system, NPC, co-player, audience.

question: How long is the anticipation built before a big physics payoff?
pole_low: Payoff comes fast; setups are quick and the crash arrives within moments
pole_high: Long build: the setup is constructed and talked up for minutes before release
why: Anticipation is the Disaster Engineer's main tool. The ratio of build-talk to payoff length is a learnable rhythm that decides whether spectacle feels earned.
evidence_needed: For each major destruction event, measure seconds of setup/narration before it vs seconds of payoff shown.

question: How directly is the audience talked to and given a job?
pole_low: Audience is a silent witness; almost no direct address
pole_high: Constant direct address: viewers suggest challenges, vote, and are answered by name or as a group
why: Viewer-driven challenges are core to Neotastic-style shows and map directly onto the Coach seat — the audience having a job is our whole product premise.
evidence_needed: Count direct-address and viewer-tasking lines per 10 minutes in sampled videos; note viewer-suggested segments.

question: How much is explained for a first-time viewer who has never seen this game?
pole_low: Assumes fluency; jargon and systems go unexplained
pole_high: Every system is named and explained in simple words as it appears
why: Clever middle-schoolers are new to most games they watch. High clarity without talking down is the lane's signature teaching skill.
evidence_needed: First-appearance explanations: when a new mechanic/mod/vehicle appears, is it explained in one simple sentence?

question: Do the stakes escalate inside a single video?
pole_low: One challenge at one difficulty, repeated or completed
pole_high: Each round is bigger, faster, or more destructive than the last
why: Escalating rounds (bigger ship, taller tower, more TNT) are how this lane holds a young viewer to the end. An avatar needs a built-in escalation instinct.
evidence_needed: Segment a video into rounds/attempts and score relative scale or difficulty of each; check for a rising pattern.

question: How much downtime survives between highlights?
pole_low: Tight: travel, building, and waiting are cut or sped past
pole_high: Loose: long unedited stretches of building, driving, or sailing remain
why: These are edited shows, so their surviving downtime tells us what our live avatar must fill — and what it can safely let breathe.
evidence_needed: Compare full videos against any available unedited/VOD versions; measure longest continuous low-action stretch kept in the edit.

question: How competent is the presented persona?
pole_low: Proudly clueless: the fun is not knowing what a button does until it is pressed
pole_high: Expert operator: deep mod, vehicle, and systems knowledge shown off
why: A clever-kid audience respects real expertise (mods, physics, aviation in PTFS/Stormworks) but also loves the reckless amateur. The avatar's claimed competence colours every line.
evidence_needed: Moments of demonstrated expert knowledge vs played-up ignorance per video; how mistakes are framed (genuine vs performed).

question: In multiplayer videos, is the creator a leader directing others or one voice in an ensemble?
pole_low: Ensemble peer: scenes and chaos emerge from the group equally
pole_high: Director: assigns roles, calls the plan, and narrates over the group
why: Coach Player inverts this: our human directs and the avatar performs. Knowing which role the winners play tells us what the avatar should expect from its coach.
evidence_needed: Multiplayer segments: who proposes the plan, who assigns roles, whose voice narrates outcomes. Tally per creator.

question: How much running scorekeeping is there — counts, scores, records, tallies?
pole_low: No numbers: events are just experienced and left behind
pole_high: Constant tally: deaths, costs, survivors, records are counted aloud and compared
why: Gray-style running counts turn chaos into a sport a kid can follow. A tally habit gives the avatar a cheap, endless source of meaningful lines.
evidence_needed: Count numeric callouts and comparisons to earlier numbers per 10 minutes in sampled videos.

question: At a big moment, does the reaction lead the event or follow it?
pole_low: Reacts after: a beat of seeing, then the response lands
pole_high: Reacts over and before: narration rides the event and predicts it as it unfolds
why: MoreAliA-style reaction timing — riding a clip with live prediction — differs from the stunned pause after a collapse. The avatar's reaction latency is a core personality parameter.
evidence_needed: Align transcript timestamps to the big in-game event: first reaction word before, during, or after the peak moment.

question: How much does the show remember and call back to earlier videos or attempts?
pole_low: Every video is a fresh start with no memory
pole_high: Dense callbacks: recurring characters, past disasters, running records and grudges
why: Callbacks are what turn viewers into regulars and what make an avatar feel like it has a life. This measures how much memory the personality layer must surface.
evidence_needed: Count references to events not contained in the current video (named recurring characters, past attempts, records) per video.

question: How willingly does the creator break their own creation or plan?
pole_low: Protective: builds carefully and tries to keep things intact
pole_high: Sacrificial: happily destroys the build, vehicle, or city the moment it is funnier
why: The willingness to sink your own ship is the soul of the sailing/disaster cluster. A protective avatar and a sacrificial one give a coach opposite games.
evidence_needed: Segments where the creator could preserve a build/vehicle but chooses the destructive option; note how the choice is narrated.

question: Is bigger always treated as better?
pole_low: Scale-neutral: small, precise experiments get equal attention
pole_high: Maximum scale worship: biggest ship, tallest tower, largest explosion is always the goal
why: Superlative scale is this lane's headline language (and MoreAliA's framing). It decides what the avatar proposes when a coach gives it freedom.
evidence_needed: Premise statements and mid-run upgrade choices: how often is the chosen next step simply a larger version of the last?

question: What fills the slow parts: teaching, story, banter, or hype maintenance?
pole_low: Utility fill: explains systems, reads comments, plans the next step
pole_high: Performance fill: bits, characters, stories, and jokes unrelated to the immediate task
why: Our avatar's hardest live problem is the quiet sail between events. This identifies which fill strategy this lane's winners actually rely on.
evidence_needed: Code every low-action 30s stretch by fill type: explanation, planning, story/bit, direct audience talk, silence.

question: How does a video end: on the biggest payoff, or with a wind-down and a next-time hook?
pole_low: Ends at the peak: final crash or result, then out
pole_high: Structured close: recap, favourite moment, and a tease of the next challenge
why: Session endings teach our avatar how to close a coached run so a kid wants another one — recap and hook are coachable rituals.
evidence_needed: Last 60s of sampled videos: presence of recap, superlative verdict, next-video tease, or abrupt end at payoff.

question: How sacred are the challenge's own stated rules?
pole_low: Rules are law: breaking one invalidates the attempt
pole_high: Rules are a starting joke: cheating, mods, and loopholes are part of the fun
why: A coach will test the avatar's rules constantly. Winners in this lane often win by bending; the avatar needs a known, legible stance on rule-bending.
evidence_needed: Challenge videos: instances of rule-bending or mod use, and whether it is hidden, confessed, or celebrated.

question: How much does the creator narrate the physics itself — forces, weight, buoyancy, speed?
pole_low: Physics is invisible: only outcomes are described (it sank, it flew, it broke)
pole_high: Physics is the commentary: predictions and explanations in cause-and-effect terms
why: For a tech-curious middle-school audience, cause-and-effect narration is the educational gold in this lane — and Neotastic/Jesse's ship and aircraft content is full of candidate material.
evidence_needed: Physics-event segments: proportion of lines containing a causal/mechanical explanation vs pure outcome description.

question: How much voice and character performance goes into NPCs and co-players?
pole_low: Everyone is referred to plainly, in the creator's normal voice
pole_high: Full character work: named personalities, voices, motives, and ongoing storylines for game characters
why: Naming and voicing NPCs turns a sandbox into a cast. It is a cheap, powerful move for our avatar — if this lane's winners actually do it.
evidence_needed: Count NPCs given names/backstories/voices per video and whether they recur across segments.

question: Where do challenges come from: the creator, the audience, or the game itself?
pole_low: Self-authored: the creator invents every premise alone
pole_high: Audience-authored: viewer comments and community suggestions drive the premises
why: If winners let the audience author premises, then coaching (our core interaction) is proven content, not just a control scheme.
evidence_needed: Premise attributions in intros and descriptions: creator idea, viewer comment shown/credited, or in-game objective.

question: How are near-misses treated compared with full successes and failures?
pole_low: Near-misses are skipped over; only clean outcomes count
pole_high: Near-misses get the biggest reaction: the almost-crash is the prized moment
why: Physics games generate constant near-misses. An avatar that can prize an almost-disaster has far more material than one waiting for clean outcomes.
evidence_needed: Identify near-miss events (close call, partial collapse) and measure reaction length/intensity vs nearby successes and failures.

question: How central are mods, cheats, and custom content to the show?
pole_low: Vanilla first: the base game as designed is the content
pole_high: Mod-driven: custom vehicles, maps, and tools are the whole point
why: Teardown/Stormworks/Roblox in this lane run on community creations. A mod-positive avatar proposes different sessions than a vanilla purist — and clever kids care about the tooling.
evidence_needed: Proportion of sampled videos whose premise requires a mod/custom map/custom vehicle; how mods are credited on screen.

question: What is the default speaking register for a young audience?
pole_low: Playground plain: mostly simple everyday words, slang-light, school-safe by instinct
pole_high: Deliberately polished presenter voice: clean, broadcast-style, no-swearing as a stated brand rule
why: Both poles are family-safe but they feel different: a mate vs a presenter. Our avatar's register must be chosen, not defaulted — MoreAliA's stated no-swearing positioning is one pole's proof.
evidence_needed: Language sampling plus any explicit channel statements about family-friendly policy; code register in openings vs mid-video.

question: How many attempts at the same challenge are shown?
pole_low: One-and-done: a single attempt, win or lose, then move on
pole_high: Many attempts: repeated tries with adjustments shown as a montage of learning
why: Repeated attempts are where a coached agent shines — each try visibly shaped by feedback. This measures whether the lane's audience tolerates iteration.
evidence_needed: Per challenge, count distinct attempts shown and whether changes between attempts are narrated.

question: How gleefully does the creator play the villain inside the game's world?
pole_low: Heroic/helpful stance: rescues, builds, and protects are the default stories
pole_high: Proud villain: sabotage, disasters, and tormenting the simulation are celebrated
why: Gray's villain-narrator stance is a huge personality attractor for this age group — and the axis our product must consciously bound, since our avatar's humour may not be cruel at people. Measure first, then cap knowingly.
evidence_needed: Stance coding of premises and reactions: helping vs harming framing of the creator's in-game actions, per creator (expect a Gray-vs-OMB split).

question: How heavily does the framing rely on superlatives — biggest, fastest, most, worst, first?
pole_low: Plain framing: a thing is done, without ranking it against everything
pole_high: Superlative-saturated: nearly every premise and reaction is framed as an extreme
why: Superlatives are this lane's headline grammar (most-viewed, biggest-ever). They are also a dial a kid can hear working — an ideal visible nudge target.
evidence_needed: Count superlative constructions in titles, thumbnails text, and the first 60s of narration per video.

question: Is silence ever allowed at a tense moment?
pole_low: No silence: every gap is filled, even during crashes and suspense
pole_high: Strategic silence: the creator shuts up and lets a sinking, fall, or approach play out
why: Zero-dead-air is this lane's reputation, but a held silence before impact may be its secret weapon. Our avatar needs a measured answer, not an assumption.
evidence_needed: Audio gap analysis around peak events: longest speech gaps in the 10s before/after impacts, compared with baseline gaps.

question: In roleplay content, how planned is the story versus improvised in the moment?
pole_low: Fully improvised: scenes happen and the story is whatever emerged
pole_high: Scenario-planned: roles, incidents, and plot beats are set up in advance
why: OMB's recording-team roleplay only works at some planning level. This tells our avatar how much scene structure a coach should supply vs leave to emergence.
evidence_needed: Roleplay videos: evidence of pre-set scenarios (assigned roles, staged incidents, stated story goals) vs purely reactive scenes.

question: How much does the creator perform a larger-than-life version of themselves?
pole_low: Ordinary person playing: minimal persona, reactions are the product
pole_high: Full self-mythology: a titled, branded character (disaster artist, chaos king) with an ongoing legend
why: A performed legend gives an avatar an identity a kid can describe in one sentence. This axis decides whether our avatar needs a title and a myth, or a face and a voice.
evidence_needed: Channel self-descriptions and in-video self-references: persona titles, claimed reputations, recurring personal legends.

question: How much real agency does the format hand to its young audience beyond watching?
pole_low: Audience influence is cosmetic: likes and comments are acknowledged only
pole_high: Audience genuinely steers: suggestions become builds, challenges, roles, and outcomes
why: This is the direct ancestor of our coach mechanic. The higher winners sit, the stronger the evidence that handing kids the steering is the entertainment, not a distraction from it.
evidence_needed: Trace 5 audience suggestions per channel from comment to on-screen outcome; count how many actually changed a video.

question: How much commentary is pure sensory narration of what is visibly happening?
pole_low: Low narration of the obvious: commentary adds plans, jokes, or analysis beyond the picture
pole_high: High play-by-play: most lines describe the visible action as it happens
why: Young viewers and second-screen watching reward play-by-play, but clever kids may find pure description empty. The ratio is a foundational avatar setting.
evidence_needed: Code 100 consecutive commentary lines per creator: describes visible action vs adds information, plan, humour, or story.

question: How much of the energy comes from rivalry — versus friends, the game, or a record?
pole_low: No rival: the contest is against the game, physics, or the creator's own past results
pole_high: Rival-driven: beating a named friend, team, or opponent is the emotional engine
why: Unspeakable-style friend-group challenges run on rivalry; solo disaster channels run on records. Our avatar's competitive target changes its trash-talk, stakes, and warmth.
evidence_needed: Premise and reaction coding: who or what is framed as the opponent in challenges across sampled videos.

question: During building or setup phases, does the creator teach the craft or entertain through it?
pole_low: Craft talk: choices explained — why this hull, this engine, this layout
pole_high: Entertainment talk: the build is a backdrop for jokes, stories, and audience chat
why: Stormworks/Teardown building phases are long. For tech-curious kids the craft talk may be the point; this decides what our avatar does with its hands busy.
evidence_needed: Build-phase transcripts coded line by line: design rationale vs unrelated entertainment content.

question: After a total disaster, how fast does the show reset and go again?
pole_low: Lingers: mourns, inspects the wreck, and debriefs before moving on
pole_high: Instant reset: laughs and immediately reloads for the next attempt
why: Reset speed is session rhythm. A debriefing avatar teaches reflection (and our owner-rite edits); an instant-reset avatar maximises attempts per session.
evidence_needed: Time from disaster peak to the start of the next attempt/segment across sampled failures.

question: How literally does the video deliver what its title and premise promised?
pole_low: Loose: the title is a vibe; the video wanders well beyond it
pole_high: Literal: the promised experiment or challenge is exactly what is delivered and judged
why: Premise honesty is trust with a young audience. It also defines our coach contract: when a kid orders a premise, how literally must the avatar honour it?
evidence_needed: Compare title/premise claims against delivered content for 3 videos per creator; score fulfilment and note digressions.

question: How often does the creator stop to be genuinely impressed by the game itself?
pole_low: Never impressed: the game is raw material and everything is a joke or a tool
pole_high: Frequent genuine wonder: pauses to admire physics, detail, or a community creation on its own merits
why: Wonder is the emotion that makes tech-curious kids fall for a simulation — and the easiest for a hype-trained avatar to lose. This axis guards the avatar's sincerity.
evidence_needed: Segments of un-ironic praise for the game/mod/creation, distinguished from hype by follow-up detail; count and duration per video.
